# The incumbent for Ateles: ad-hoc agent invocation by hand

## Subject

What the ICP (solo technical founder-operator) actually uses today before adopting Ateles: no vendor, no competing platform — direct, unattributed invocation of coding-agent CLIs (claude, similar), coordinated entirely by the operator's own memory and typing.

## Summary

The reader's actual current solution, in their own vocabulary: opening a chat (or several) with claude / Claude Code by hand per task, re-explaining context each session because nothing persists between them, running agents under the operator's own identity with no distinct attribution (a code-writing agent acts as the operator on GitHub with no audit trail tying the signed subject to the action), approving risky actions ad hoc in the chat itself rather than through any declared checkpoint, and accumulating coordination logic as a growing CLAUDE.md plus scattered shell scripts and one-off Python rather than any declared workflow. Failure modes, concretely: (1) zero-context restarts — every session starts from nothing, so the operator re-explains project state, prior decisions, and constraints each time; (2) identity collapse — there is one shared bearer (the operator's own login/keys), so a merge, a payment, or an outbound message done by an agent is indistinguishable after the fact from one done by the operator, and there is no reconstructable record of who authorized what; (3) manual sequencing — running more than one agent means opening multiple chats and hoping they do not conflict, which is bespoke integration work the operator pays for every time a new domain is added; (4) no standing memory — what one session learns is not available to the next, so facts and decisions are re-derived or silently lost; (5) instructions as governance — CLAUDE.md-style prose accretes as the only enforcement mechanism, which is advisory, not binding: nothing fails when it is violated, so it is documentation, not a control.

Cross-checked against README.md's 'Why this exists' section (origin/main), which lists the same failure modes as the motivating problem.

## Conclusion

WHAT ATELES RESOLVES: identity collapse (agents carry AAuth-signed identities distinct from the operator, with every write attributed to the principal it acted for); manual sequencing across domains (one dispatch/claim mechanism rather than per-chat coordination, so adding a domain does not add a second system to run); cross-process, cross-day standing memory as modelled, attributable, correctable RECORD rather than mere recoverable state (Neotoma as one durable, typed, provenance-tracked graph any daemon or runner reads/writes, detailed below); advisory-only governance (declared workflows and gates that mechanically block — a mechanism that does not bind is not a control — rather than prose an agent may or may not follow). WHAT IT DOES NOT RESOLVE: Ateles is a reference architecture you fork and adapt, not an installable product — it does not remove the requirement to read Python, provision keypairs/secrets, and run your own daemons; it does not serve teams or multi-operator organizations (P2-P5 multi-operator authority is designed but unbuilt, per docs/foundation/status.md); it does not offer zero-install onboarding: someone who wants to sign up rather than fork gets no path in.

THE COMPETITOR TEST, RE-RUN AGAINST SHIPPING CAPABILITY (updated 2026-09-21, second pass): each failure mode was checked against what LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen actually ship today (see method for the exact source files/docs read), using the register's own boundary (plan ent_98ef9d45f8a6896fed408f8f decision 'positioning_categories'; restated in README.md's 'How does this compare to LangGraph / CrewAI / AutoGen?': those frameworks orchestrate multi-step LLM calls inside ONE process and coordinate computation; Ateles coordinates long-running background daemons and per-task runners, each with its own signed identity, writing to a canonical record — governed fleets across days, not chains across seconds) as the discriminator, not a feature checklist.

- ZERO-CONTEXT RESTARTS and NO STANDING MEMORY — RESTATED, not borderline, and not primarily on reach. The PRIMARY discriminator is KIND OF STATE, not scope: a checkpointer or memory store persists EXECUTION/RECALL STATE — where a run got to, or a retrievable trace of past interaction — not a MODELLED, TYPED, ATTRIBUTABLE, CORRECTABLE RECORD that is meaningful to a reader who never saw the process that wrote it. Verified directly against source, not assumed: LangGraph's `Item` class (libs/checkpoint/langgraph/store/base/__init__.py, langchain-ai/langgraph) stores `value: dict[str, Any]` — an arbitrary, schema-less, developer-defined blob — plus `key`/`namespace`/`created_at`/`updated_at`. There is no author/attribution field and no supersession semantics: `updated_at` marks the last write, but the prior value is not retained, versioned, or queryable as history. Checkpointer state is stricter still: it is the graph's own developer-defined state object, scoped to and legible only to that graph. CrewAI's `MemoryRecord` (lib/crewai/src/crewai/memory/types.py, crewAIInc/crewAI) confirms the same shape: `content: str` (free text) plus an untyped `metadata: dict[str, Any]`, a `source: str | None` field documented as "for provenance tracking," but this is a single origin tag (e.g. 'user:alice'), not per-field attribution or an audit trail, and there is no separate typed "entity memory" in the current codebase — CrewAI's own docs confirm the earlier short-term/long-term/entity split was collapsed into one untyped `Memory` class. Consolidation on a duplicate is explicitly LLM-arbitrated keep/update/delete (the update path overwrites, it does not retain the superseded value). So: NEITHER framework offers a typed domain-entity model, per-field attribution recording who wrote a value under what authority, or correction semantics that retain a superseded value alongside its replacement. A checkpointer/store fanned out across every process and day would still answer "where did this run get to" or "what does this text vaguely resemble," not "what is true, who said so, and what did it used to be" — which is what Ateles's claim (coordinating legitimate action: who authorized what, against which state) actually requires, since you cannot ask a checkpointer or a memory record who authorized a payment when neither has a concept of "payment," "authorization," or a typed, correctable field for either. The PROCESS/HORIZON argument (thread-scoped vs. cross-process, single-run vs. cross-day) is a real and independently-confirmed consequence of this — LangGraph's own docs say checkpointers are not for cross-process use and route cross-thread needs to Store, and CrewAI's memory is scoped to one crew's local run directory — but it is downstream of the kind-of-state gap, not the primary reason the mode survives: state only the writing run/thread can interpret cannot usefully cross tools regardless of how far you widen its reach, because nothing else could read it as a typed thing. Restated failure mode: "there is no shared, typed, attributable, correctable model of the domain — only untyped execution/recall state scoped to the process or thread that wrote it" — that is what Ateles resolves (Neotoma's entities are typed, versioned via priority-ordered observations, provenance-tracked per field, and correctable in place with both old and new retained) and neither framework ships.

- MANUAL SEQUENCING — RESTATED as a PUSH VS. PULL distinction (operator-directed re-test, 2026-09-21, third pass), not dropped and not borderline. The prior DROP conflated two different questions: whether agents can be sequenced inside a run (they can, and these frameworks do it well) and HOW an executor is selected for a step. Checked against primary source, not documentation prose: CrewAI's own execution loop (`_execute_tasks` in crew.py, crewAIInc/crewAI) iterates `self.tasks` and calls `task.execute_sync(agent=exec_data.agent, ...)` — the crew, a central orchestrating object, resolves and hands each task to an agent object; the agent performs no "is this mine" fitness judgment and holds no lease the crew reads back before assigning. In hierarchical mode this is explicit: `_create_manager_agent` instantiates a manager agent with `allow_delegation=True` whose job is to delegate tasks to the other agents — a push by construction. LangGraph's scheduler (`prepare_next_tasks` in `libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_algo.py`, langchain-ai/langgraph) unilaterally computes, from graph topology and per-node `triggers` against updated channel versions, the set of `PregelTask`s to run next each superstep; a node never chooses to take work, and dynamic dispatch via `Send` is materialized through an internal constant literally named `PUSH_TRIGGER`. (LangGraph's `PULL` task-path tag names the *data-flow direction* — a node reads its input from subscribed channels — not an accountable claim: there is no persisted holder read back before the scheduler accepts a task as taken, checked specifically to rule out a false match on the name.) AutoGen's `SelectorGroupChatManager` (`_selector_group_chat.py`, microsoft/autogen) selects the next speaker with a ChatCompletion model call inside the manager itself — a 1:N inference in an actor that neither acts on nor answers for a misroute, the exact fallthrough hazard `work_model.md#pull-is-the-only-delivery-assignment-constrains-eligibility` names. None of the three frameworks has a claim/lease primitive anywhere in this path: no persisted lease with a holder read back after the write (`work_model.md#the-claim-and-the-lease-are-one-primitive`), no `assigned_to`-as-eligibility distinct from a holder (`work_model.md#assignment-restricts-eligibility-it-never-creates-a-lease`), and no analogue of an `unspawnable_assignee` checkpoint for a routing decision that resolves to nobody accountable. This is a genuinely different failure mode from the one dropped, not the same one restated: "sequencing agents in a run" is a coordination-convenience claim these frameworks answer directly; "work is pushed by a router/manager/scheduler that cannot be held accountable for a misroute, versus claimed by the principal that answers for the outcome" is an accountability claim none of them make any provision for. It is also not redundant with the two modes that already SURVIVE: identity collapse is about whether an executed action is attributable to a distinct signed principal after the fact, and advisory-only governance is about whether a declared gate mechanically binds — neither is about how the executor for a step gets selected in the first place. Restated failure mode, replacing the dropped one: "the framework's own scheduler, crew, or manager selects and pushes the next executor by topology, delegation, or model inference, with no claim a principal makes for itself and no lease an executor holds that the dispatcher must read back — so a wrong selection reaches an executor with nobody accountable for the choice." What Ateles resolves against it (`work_model.md#pull-is-the-only-delivery-assignment-constrains-eligibility` through `#the-claim-and-the-lease-are-one-primitive`): work reaches an agent only by its own claim, `assigned_to` narrows eligibility without ever installing a holder, and the claim and the lease are one primitive whose holder is read back after the write — so exclusivity and accountability are the same fact, not two.

- IDENTITY COLLAPSE — SURVIVES, unchanged from the prior test, and reinforced by the same kind-of-state gap above: neither framework's Item/MemoryRecord has a field for "which principal authorized this under what scope" — `source` on a CrewAI record is an origin tag on a text blob, not a signed, distinct, per-agent identity backing a typed action. None of the three frameworks model authority, accountability, or per-agent signed identity distinct from execution; they coordinate computation, not legitimate action.

- INSTRUCTIONS AS GOVERNANCE (advisory-only) — SURVIVES, unchanged. None of the three frameworks offer mechanically-binding gates; tool-allowlists and prompts in all of them are advisory in-code, enforced (if at all) by a separate sandbox/data layer the frameworks themselves do not provide.

CANDIDATES ELIMINATED, RESTATED, OR DEMOTED ACROSS BOTH RE-RUNS: manual sequencing, initially dropped outright as framing the competitor's own category, is on further operator-directed test (push vs. pull, third pass) RESTATED rather than dropped — see above; the coordination-convenience version of the claim is correctly conceded to the frameworks, but a distinct accountability claim about how the executor is selected survives under primary-source evidence none of the three frameworks answer. Zero-context restarts and no standing memory are restated with kind-of-state (typed/attributable/correctable record vs. untyped execution/recall state) as the primary discriminator and process/horizon as its downstream consequence — at the literal original wording a shipping framework could otherwise claim a persistence feature exists, which is why kind-of-state rather than mere reach is the correct test. Identity collapse and advisory-only governance are unchanged and remain failure modes that survive without restatement from the second pass, and identity collapse is reinforced by the same evidence; the push/pull restatement of manual sequencing is a distinct fourth surviving mode, not a restatement of either.

FOURTH PASS (2026-09-21, operator-directed): Claude Projects, ChatGPT, and Grok tested against what each ships today, per method above. Verdicts use the surviving two-boundary vocabulary — KIND OF STATE (recall vs. record: does the competitor persist a typed, attributable, correctable RECORD, or only prose/execution/recall state?) and PUSH VS. PULL (does work reach an executor by routing/handoff with no claim/lease read-back, or by the executor's own claim against a persisted, read-back lease?) — replacing the old "no concept of payment or authorization" formulation, which fails against prose memory that can trivially contain a sentence naming an authorized payment without it being a queryable, correctable fact.

**CLAUDE PROJECTS**

- KIND OF STATE — RESTATED, per the peer session's analysis (ent_48bfa9047aa4489204ca0d1f), carried forward: Projects' `MEMORY.md` is agent-written prose, read at thread start, stored in Anthropic's project store. It is a cache with good ergonomics, not a record — no schema, no per-field attribution, and the peer analysis notes a project (with its memory) cannot be shared or moved, so even where content happens to be correct it is not independently queryable as a typed fact the way a Neotoma entity field is. RESTATED rather than SURVIVES-unchanged because, unlike LangGraph/CrewAI, Projects' memory is closer in shape to Ateles's own prose-risk (agent-written text that COULD contain an authorization-like sentence) — the discriminator that holds is the same recall-vs-record test, not scope.
- PUSH VS. PULL — SURVIVES, confirmed by both the peer analysis and this pass's own reading of the source docs: Projects routes ("Claude decides where each message you send in the conversation goes... Claude tells you which"), a 1:N inference in the coordinator, and the doc's own troubleshooting section ("Threads guessed or stalled instead of asking") is the fallthrough failure observed in a shipped system by its own authors — independent, stronger evidence than an internal argument.
- IDENTITY COLLAPSE / AUTHORITY — SURVIVES, confirmed by cloud-environments and claude-code-on-the-web (fetched fresh this pass): threads inherit the operator's GitHub App installation and connector credentials wholesale; there is no principal+domain+scope+action+conditions+time tuple, no expiry, no attenuation on an approval beyond "the rest of that thread." Credential protection (scoped proxy, keys outside the sandbox) is real infrastructure hygiene but is not an authority MODEL — it protects the secret, not the scope of its use.
- ADVISORY GOVERNANCE — SURVIVES, per the peer analysis and confirmed unchanged: project instructions are, in the vendor's own words, "instructions Claude keeps to, not enforced settings."

Self-criticisms verified this pass, all four holding:
(a) Sandbox-per-thread beats a discipline rule — VERIFIED. claude-code-on-the-web, "Security and isolation": "Isolated virtual machines: each session runs in an isolated, Anthropic-managed VM." Worktrees are named in the peer analysis as what Projects threads structurally do not need; Ateles's "one worktree, one agent" is an operator rule violated in this repo the same day this finding was corrected — per `principles.md` invariant 1, a rule nothing enforces is not a control, and this is a case where Projects enforces structurally what Ateles enforces by prose.
(b) Auto-fix owned-through-merge is shipped — VERIFIED verbatim from claude-code-on-the-web: "Claude subscribes to GitHub activity on the PR, and when a check fails or a reviewer leaves a comment, Claude investigates and pushes a fix if one is clear... Claude may reply to review comment threads on GitHub as part of resolving them." This is real, shipped, and ahead of what Ateles's own principle 10 ("handing work to the swarm is not completion") argues for but only partly implements per `status.md` (nothing tracks a PR from open to deployed).
(c) THE BIG ONE, authority enforcement — VERIFIED against `docs/foundation/charter.md` at origin/main, objective 2, read in full this pass: the document states, of its own authority model, "the model is the most complete thing in the corpus and the least enforced," and directs a reader who wants to know what is enforced TODAY to `status.md`, "and the answer there is not the same answer." `status.md`'s own table under `authority_model.md` (not reproduced in full here; see the document) lists five fail-open paths. So a claim of the shape "Ateles has an authority model and Projects doesn't" is true only as a designed-for/not-designed-for comparison; "we have this and they don't," read as a claim about what is running, is the exact overclaim the charter itself refutes. The correct claim, preserved: Ateles's authority model is DESIGNED to bind at every action (principal+domain+scope+action+conditions+time, default-deny, revocable); Projects' is not designed to at all (no tuple exists to enforce). Whether Ateles's design currently binds in a given checkout is a `status.md` question, not a corpus-design question, and the two must not be conflated in any external-facing claim.
(d) Projects not attempting legitimacy is coherent — VERIFIED against `status.md`'s roadmap table (read fresh this pass): P2 multi-operator identity is "designed... except `multi_tenant.md` section 7; nothing built; no principal entity has a runtime reader"; P3 delegation/approval is "design stated; nothing built"; P4 is "object set decided; eight questions open... awaiting the operator." So Ateles's own plural-principal (P2-P5) case is designed but unbuilt — the honest framing is two designs answering different questions (Projects: single operator, all six authority questions resolve to "the user"; Ateles: designed for plural principals, not yet built there either), not "a worse answer to the same question."

**CHATGPT**

- KIND OF STATE — DROPPED as inapplicable in the form tested for LangGraph/CrewAI/Projects, RESTATED as recall-vs-record: ChatGPT's memory (help.openai.com/en/articles/8590148-memory-faq, fetched 2026-09-21) is explicitly prose ("a high-level view"), explicitly mutable-by-relevance rather than stable ("can change as ChatGPT updates what is most useful to remember"), and its correction mechanism is suppression, not correction-with-retained-history: "Don't mention this again reduces future references to the information. It does not delete the original source." There is no field, no schema, no attribution of which of several possible sources wrote a value, and no versioned "old value retained alongside new" semantics anywhere in the documented mechanism. RESTATED verdict: SURVIVES. This is the sharpest confirmation yet of the recall-vs-record distinction, because ChatGPT memory is precisely the "agent-written prose that can trivially contain 'the operator authorized the payment on the 14th'" case the operator named as the reason the old formulation fails — and it still fails the record test, because that sentence, even if present, is not a queryable typed fact, has no per-field authority attached, and a correction to it is documented as suppression of future mention, not as an update that retains the superseded value.

- PUSH VS. PULL — CORRECTED, FIFTH PASS (2026-09-21, operator-directed re-test of a named gap). The fourth pass's "DOES NOT APPLY" verdict was WRONG and is now SURVIVES. The fourth pass's own confidence field named the exact hole that broke it: "Codex automations are named but not read in this pass... and are an explicit gap," alongside "Medium that no OTHER ChatGPT surface... exists that would reintroduce the push/pull question." That gap was read this pass and it reintroduces the question. Primary source, fetched and read in full 2026-09-21 (both via WebFetch and independently confirmed by direct browser render of the same URL, so this is not a single-fetch artifact): https://learn.chatgpt.com/codex/agent-configuration/subagents (note: developers.openai.com/codex/* now 308-redirects to learn.chatgpt.com/docs/*, a domain migration the fourth pass could not have known about). Verbatim: "ChatGPT Work and Codex can run subagent workflows by spawning specialized agents in parallel and then collecting their results in one response." "Subagent: A delegated agent that Codex starts to handle a specific task." "Current Codex releases enable subagent workflows by default" — shipped and on by default, not announced-only. Decision mechanics, verbatim: "ChatGPT or Codex handles orchestration across agents, including spawning new subagents, routing follow-up instructions, waiting for results, and closing agent threads." This is push by construction: the parent agent (or, on Ultra reasoning effort, the model itself via "proactive delegation," where "ChatGPT can delegate suitable independent work without explicit requests") decides to spawn, selects which custom agent configuration (TOML file under `~/.codex/agents/` or `.codex/agents/`, each with `name`/`description`/`developer_instructions`) or built-in agent (`default`, `worker`, `explorer`) to use, and routes instructions to it — structurally identical to CrewAI's `_execute_tasks`/`allow_delegation` manager-push and LangGraph's `PUSH_TRIGGER` scheduler already found to fail this boundary in the second/third pass. No claim/lease primitive was found anywhere on the page: subagents do not evaluate whether work is theirs, do not hold or read back a persisted lease, and are not described as claiming anything — they are configured and spawned. This is the identical test already run against LangGraph/CrewAI/AutoGen, applied faithfully rather than waved off. The first sentence of the page — "ChatGPT Work and Codex can run subagent workflows" — also means the fourth pass's premise for Work specifically ("Work is a per-conversation mode toggle... not a router across parallel worker threads") is now incomplete: Work shares the same subagent push-delegation mechanism as Codex, confirmed on a re-fetch of help.openai.com/en/articles/20001275-chatgpt-work-and-codex this pass (page now shows "Updated: 5 days ago," i.e. materially revised since the fourth pass's read — the "Codex automations run in Codex" sentence the fourth pass quoted from this page no longer appears in the current revision; Work remains framed as a Chat/Work/Codex toggle on this page, but the separate subagents page establishes the routing mechanism the fourth pass could not find here). Operator's challenge ("Doesn't ChatGPT Codex or Work or both have the notion of subagents with routing?") was correct: the answer is yes for both, via one shared mechanism, and the prior verdict was wrong because the named surface (Codex automations, and by extension the sibling subagents page one click from the Codex overview) went unread rather than found-absent.

- IDENTITY COLLAPSE — not directly tested this pass (ChatGPT's docs read did not cover GitHub App / connector credential architecture the way Claude's or Grok's did); flagged as NOT VERIFIED, not asserted either way.
- ADVISORY GOVERNANCE — not directly tested this pass for the same reason; NOT VERIFIED.

**GROK (Grok Bot, xAI/Cursor)**

- KIND OF STATE — SURVIVES. docs.x.ai/grok-bot/overview FAQ, verbatim: "What does a Bot remember? Stable preferences, role context, and summaries of prior work... For consequential decisions, ask the Bot to check the current source instead of relying on memory." This is vendor-documented recall state with an explicit warning against treating it as a record — the clearest self-admission of the recall/record distinction found in any of the six competitors now tested. No schema, no field-level attribution, no correction-with-history semantics are documented anywhere on either page read.
- PUSH VS. PULL — SURVIVES, but on different evidence than the frameworks: Grok Bot's own docs describe "pass ownership of a task" as a Bot-to-Bot or group-chat MESSAGE — an informal handoff, not a scheduler/router process — with no persisted lease and no read-back of a holder anywhere in the two pages read. Because Bots message each other directly rather than a central process routing to them, this is not the identical fallthrough shape as Projects/LangGraph/AutoGen/Codex (there is no third-party router inferring a bad match), but it still has no claim/lease primitive: a Bot receiving "ownership" via message has made no accountable claim against a persisted eligibility record, and nothing reads back who currently holds a task before treating a handoff as final. RESTATED to note the shape is informal-handoff rather than router-fallthrough, but the underlying gap — no persisted, read-back claim/lease — is the same one `work_model.md` names.
- IDENTITY COLLAPSE — SURVIVES, and this is the strongest, most directly on-point evidence found in this entire competitor test, verified verbatim from docs.x.ai/grok-bot/security (dated 2026-09-17): "A Bot has no identity or credentials of its own: Bots act as the signed-in member. A Bot can never hold more access than the person it belongs to, every action stays attributable to a named member, and there is no separate machine identity outside your identity provider to provision, rotate, or audit." This is the shared-bearer design the charter names as the failure Ateles resolves ("nothing an agent does is untraceable to whoever it acted for... a shared bearer is not attribution"), except Grok Bot documents it as an intentional design choice rather than a gap, with one named exception (team-managed connectors using team/service-account credentials). "Every action stays attributable to a named member" is real and should not be understated — it is stronger than "untraceable" — but it attributes to the HUMAN member, not to a distinct signed agent principal, so a Bot's action and the member's own action remain indistinguishable after the fact, which is exactly the charter's test.
- ADVISORY GOVERNANCE — RESTATED, evidenced more specifically than for the frameworks: Grok Bot ships Auto Review, a real binding mechanism for a defined action set (shell commands, plugin calls, computer use, automation writes, delegation) — stronger than pure prose. But the same security page states verbatim that Auto Review "does not review every side effect; memory writes and most settings changes are examples" — so the exact channel this finding's KIND-OF-STATE test depends on (memory writes) is explicitly outside the one enforcement mechanism Grok Bot has. RESTATED failure mode: governance is binding for a named action class and explicitly non-binding for memory, which is a narrower and more precise claim than "advisory-only," and a fair reader should note Grok Bot is ahead of the three frameworks and roughly level with Projects on this boundary specifically.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE A PAGE: the fourth pass's own note flagged the ChatGPT push-vs-pull "DOES NOT APPLY" and the Grok identity finding as candidates for the next page rebuild. The fifth pass corrects the first of those: ChatGPT/Codex now reads as SURVIVES on push-vs-pull, on the same footing as LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, Claude Projects, and Grok — all six competitors tested now SURVIVE push-vs-pull, none DROPPED, none DOES-NOT-APPLY. This pass did not rebuild any rendered page (research-only, per this run's explicit instruction); the corrected ChatGPT row is a candidate for the next page rebuild along with the still-outstanding Grok identity finding.
